claim: The cost for de novo drug development ranges from $3 billion to more than $30 billion.
source: Despite the major advances in drug research and development (R&D), the cost for de novo drug development remains high, ranging from $3 billion to more than $30 billion.
evidence: This claim cites a specific reference (Scannell et al., 2012) to support the stated cost range.

claim: It usually takes over 10 years to bring a new drug from bench to bedside.
source: Moreover, it usually takes over 10 years to bring a new drug from bench to bedside, reflecting the complex challenges in this area (Scannell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scannell et al., 2012.

claim: Drug repositioning can greatly shorten the gap between preclinical drug research and clinical applications.
source: Within this context, exploring new indications for existing drugs (drug-centric) or identifying effective drugs for certain diseases (disease-centric) represents an appealing concept, namely 'drug repositioning' (or 'drug repurposing'), which can greatly shorten the gap between preclinical drug research and clinical applications (Ashburn and Thor, 2004; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ashburn and Thor, 2004 and Liu et al., 2013.

claim: CMap Build 2 contains 3 cell lines and 1309 compounds.
source: These two projects have generated large-scale drug-induced gene expression profiles on multiple cancer cell lines under different treatment conditions (CMap Build 2: 3 cell lines, 1309 compounds; LINCS: 77 cell lines, 19,811 compounds), representing a treasure trove for in silico therapeutic exploration (Musa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with a citation to Musa et al., 2018.

claim: LINCS contains 77 cell lines and 19,811 compounds.
source: These two projects have generated large-scale drug-induced gene expression profiles on multiple cancer cell lines under different treatment conditions (CMap Build 2: 3 cell lines, 1309 compounds; LINCS: 77 cell lines, 19,811 compounds), representing a treasure trove for in silico therapeutic exploration (Musa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with a citation to Musa et al., 2018.

claim: LINCS represents a 1000-fold scale-up of the original CMap.
source: As a 1000-fold scale-up of the original CMap, LINCS contained dramatic increases in both cell line types and perturbations, making it the focus of the present investigation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Compounds with the ability to reverse disease-specific gene expression pattern are considered therapeutic candidates.
source: Briefly, compounds with the ability to reverse disease-specific gene expression pattern are considered therapeutic candidates (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1, with a citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: Liver cancer directly accounts for nearly one million deaths each year.
source: As one of the most lethal malignancies worldwide, liver cancer directly accounts for nearly one million deaths each year (Bray et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bray et al., 2018.

claim: Hepatocellular carcinoma represents approximately 90% of all liver cancer cases.
source: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the major type of liver cancer, representing approximately 90% of all liver cancer cases (Llovet et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Llovet et al., 2016.

claim: Most of the measurements in LINCS were made in the treatment durations of 6 hr (43%) or 24 hr (56.6%).
source: Most of the measurements were made in the treatment durations of 6 hr (43%) or 24 hr (56.6%), and under the concentrations of 5 μM (21%) or 10 μM (63%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Most of the measurements in LINCS were made under the concentrations of 5 μM (21%) or 10 μM (63%).
source: Most of the measurements were made in the treatment durations of 6 hr (43%) or 24 hr (56.6%), and under the concentrations of 5 μM (21%) or 10 μM (63%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Only 9 cell lines in LINCS contained more than 5000 profiles, which account for 77.8% of all compound profiles.
source: Although 71 cell lines were included in LINCS project in total, not all of them were extensively profiled, and only 9 cell lines contained more than 5000 profiles, which, however, account for 77.8% of all compound profiles.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: There were 2912 compounds shared by the nine most profiled cell lines in LINCS.
source: There were 2912 compounds shared by these nine cell lines.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Most compound-induced gene expression changes tended to be cell-type specific.
source: As shown in the figure, most dots with the same color clustered together, indicating that most of compound-induced gene expression changes tended to be cell-type specific.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the t-SNE plot shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A high degree of cell-specificity was observed for most compounds, with a median L2 similarity score of 0.078.
source: As a result, a high degree of cell-specificity was observed for most compounds, with a median L2 similarity score of 0.078 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Inhibitors targeting core cellular processes tend to induce similar changes across all cell lines.
source: Results suggested that inhibitors targeting core cellular processes (e.g., cell cycle, RNA transcription, and protein synthesis) tended to induce similar changes across all cell lines, generally in agreement with previous findings (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 2; Niepel et al., 2017; Subramanian et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and citations to previous studies.

claim: There was a significant, albeit not very remarkable, association between the perturbed expression similarities and basal expression similarities (ρ=0.344; p=0.040).
source: The result showed that there was a significant, albeit not very remarkable, association between the perturbed expression similarities (cell line pair-level, L4) and basal expression similarities (ρ=0.344; p=0.040), suggesting that cell lines with similar molecular features were more likely to have consistent gene expression changes upon perturbation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical values and supported by Figure 2G.

claim: PC3 cell line showed the highest L5 similarity score (median value=0.122) among the nine cell lines tested.
source: Among the nine cell lines we tested, PC3 cell line showed the highest L5 similarity score (median value=0.122) (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: HepG2 exhibited a significantly higher expression correlation with liver cancer cell lines (median correlation coefficient=0.729) compared to other tissue-derived cancer cell lines.
source: Compared to other tissue-derived cancer cell lines or normal/tumor tissues, HepG2 exhibited a significantly higher expression correlation with liver cancer cell lines (median correlation coefficient=0.729), normal liver tissues (median correlation coefficient=0.616), and liver cancer tissues (median correlation coefficient=0.631) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HepG2 exhibited a significantly higher expression correlation with normal liver tissues (median correlation coefficient=0.616) compared to other tissues.
source: Compared to other tissue-derived cancer cell lines or normal/tumor tissues, HepG2 exhibited a significantly higher expression correlation with liver cancer cell lines (median correlation coefficient=0.729), normal liver tissues (median correlation coefficient=0.616), and liver cancer tissues (median correlation coefficient=0.631) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HepG2 exhibited a significantly higher expression correlation with liver cancer tissues (median correlation coefficient=0.631) compared to other tumor tissues.
source: Compared to other tissue-derived cancer cell lines or normal/tumor tissues, HepG2 exhibited a significantly higher expression correlation with liver cancer cell lines (median correlation coefficient=0.729), normal liver tissues (median correlation coefficient=0.616), and liver cancer tissues (median correlation coefficient=0.631) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The use of LINCS-derived HepG2 data is preferable to be limited within liver diseases.
source: Collectively, we supposed that the use of LINCS-derived HepG2 data was preferable to be limited within liver diseases.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the expression correlation data presented.

claim: Statistically significant correlation could be observed between similarity scores and AUDRC values.
source: As a result, statistically significant correlation could still be observed between similarity scores and AUDRC values in these scenarios, further proving the reliability of this standard (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A benchmark data set was generated, composed of 117 unique compounds with both LINCS and drug efficacy (IC50) data available.
source: A benchmark data set was then generated, composed of 117 unique compounds with both LINCS and drug efficacy (IC50) data available, which was taken as a basis for the application of AUC-based standard (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: A set of 27 potential HCC agents were compiled which were both included in LINCS and under clinical trials for liver cancer treatment.
source: To verify this hypothesis, we compiled a set of 27 potential HCC agents which were both included in LINCS and under clinical trials for liver cancer treatment.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The HCC agent set was negatively enriched in KS test.
source: The results of KS test demonstrated that the HCC agent set was indeed negatively enriched (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: XSum outperformed other five methods across almost all candidate topNs when using SigLIRI as query signature.
source: In the condition of using SigLIRI as query signature, both benchmarking standards demonstrated that XSum outperformed other five methods across almost all candidate topNs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: XSum exhibited a consistently excellent performance, independently of the query signature and benchmarking standard.
source: Generally, XSum exhibited a consistently excellent performance, independently of the query signature and benchmarking standard (Supplementary file 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 6A and B.

claim: RGES was superior to the KS method and might serve as an alternative approach for KS-based connectivity mapping.
source: In addition, our analyses also demonstrated that the recently developed RGES (a modification of the KS method) was superior to the KS method and might serve as an alternative approach for KS-based connectivity mapping (Chen et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is based on the analyses conducted in the study and cites Chen et al., 2017a.

claim: The optimal window with the best performance was either 'top150–200' or 'top200–250'.
source: With this normalization approach, relatively consistent results across varying conditions were obtained. The optimal window with the best performance was either 'top150–200' or 'top200–250' (Supplementary file 6C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Supplementary file 6C.

claim: A topN of 200 could serve as a rough guide for applying XSum method.
source: Besides, we also observed a biphasic pattern of fitting curves, with the inflection points appearing where topNs were around 200 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F). Collectively, we supposed that topN of 200 could serve as a rough guide.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the data and figures presented.

claim: Similar trends of biphasic pattern with inflection points at around 100 could be observed under different conditions using the iterative fold change-based approach.
source: The exact sizes of optimal signatures identified by this approach varied substantially (including 55, 79, 140, and 167). Despite this, similar trends of biphasic pattern with inflection points at around 100 under different conditions could still be observed (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: As the signature sizes increased, the DR-AUC/DR-ES values also increased/decreased and eventually converged when the signature size was more than 100.
source: The results showed that, as the signature sizes increased, the DR-AUC/DR-ES values also increased/decreased and eventually converged when the signature size was more than 100 (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A signature size of 100 could be selected as a good compromise.
source: Accordingly, we considered that a signature size of 100 could be selected as a good compromise.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of data from both approaches.

claim: More than 0.90 of AUC can be obtained in seven out of the eight cohorts (87.5%) for the optimal signature's ability to distinguish tumors from non-tumors.
source: The results showed that more than 0.90 of AUC can be obtained in seven out of the eight cohorts (87.5%), indicating that the ability to discern the difference between diseased and normal states might be an indispensable property for achieving good retrieval performance (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Significant prognostic implications of the optimal signature could be observed in six out of the eight cohorts (75%).
source: As a result, significant prognostic implications of the optimal signature could be observed in six out of the eight cohorts (75%), suggesting that prognostic significance was also a necessary characteristic (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the optimal signature and multiple clinical features, including BCLC stage (p=0.011), tumor thrombus (p=0.001), AFP level (p=0.022), TNM stage (p<0.001), and histologic grade (p<0.001).
source: The results showed that there was a significant correlation between the optimal signature and multiple clinical features, including BCLC stage (p=0.011), tumor thrombus (p=0.001), AFP level (p=0.022), TNM stage (p<0.001), and histologic grade (p<0.001) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical values and supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A good query signature should possess the ability to comprehensively recapitulate the clinical features of corresponding disease.
source: Accordingly, we concluded that a good query signature should possess the ability to comprehensively recapitulate the clinical features of corresponding disease, rather than only reflect the disease characteristic from single perspective.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the analyses conducted in the study.

claim: Preliminary screening yielded a total of 6017 stage-associated genes (23.9%), of which 309 were landmark genes.
source: This screening yielded a total of 6017 stage-associated genes (23.9%), of which 309 were landmark genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Seven gene modules were discerned by WGCNA analysis.
source: Seven gene modules were discerned by WGCNA analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C), and two of them, which we termed the 'ascending' module (N=1738) and the 'descending' module (N=350) for their greatest relevance to stages and patterns of linear evolution from normal to cancer, were retained for further analyses (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The 'ascending' module was closely associated with proliferation.
source: We found that the 'ascending' module was closely associated with proliferation (Figure 6C), while the 'descending' module was enriched in several different types of processes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Sigevo is comprised of 82 ascending genes and 18 descending genes.
source: This analysis yielded a signature comprised of 82 ascending genes and 18 descending genes, which was then named as Sigevo (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Sigevo had a remarkable capability for distinguishing tumors from non-tumors, with a median AUC of 0.972 in all eight cohorts.
source: First, based on clinical cohorts of HCC, we demonstrated that Sigevo had a remarkable capability for distinguishing tumors from non-tumors, with a median AUC of 0.972 in all eight cohorts (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Sigevo held great prognostic power in HCC.
source: Besides, this signature also held great prognostic power in HCC, as indicated by the results of Cox analyses (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Sigevo could effectively differentiate between mild (S0/S1) and severe (S3/S4) fibrosis.
source: The result suggested that Sigevo could also effectively differentiate between mild (S0/S1) and severe (S3/S4) fibrosis (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Ascending genes in Sigevo were significantly enriched in both CCl4-treated and DEN-treated liver tissues.
source: It could be observed that ascending genes in Sigevo were significantly enriched in both CCl4-treated (GSE27640) and DEN-treated (GSE19057) liver tissues (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: After excluding preclinical agents or agents withdrawn from the market, 793 agents remained as repositioning candidates.
source: After excluding preclinical agents or agents withdrawn from the market, 793 agents remained (Corsello et al., 2017). These agents were then considered repositioning candidates (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with a citation to Corsello et al., 2017.

claim: Some agents which were previously proved to have chemopreventive effects, including erlotinib, caffeine, and fasudil, dominated relatively high rankings on the list.
source: Interestingly, some agents which were previously proved to have chemopreventive effects, including erlotinib (Fuchs et al., 2014), caffeine (Hoshida et al., 2012), and fasudil (Nakagawa et al., 2016), dominated relatively high rankings on the list (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with citations and supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Anti-HCC agents were found to be enriched significantly in compounds with reversal potency.
source: Besides, anti-HCC agents were also found to be enriched significantly in compounds with reversal potency (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: HHT had the highest reversal potency among 793 repositioning candidates.
source: According to the computational results, homoharringtonine (HHT) (Figure 7C), a protein synthesis inhibitor targeting RPL3, had the highest reversal potency among 793 repositioning candidates (Tujebajeva et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with a citation to Tujebajeva et al., 1989.

claim: HHT is a protein synthesis inhibitor targeting RPL3.
source: According to the computational results, homoharringtonine (HHT) (Figure 7C), a protein synthesis inhibitor targeting RPL3, had the highest reversal potency among 793 repositioning candidates (Tujebajeva et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with a citation to Tujebajeva et al., 1989.

claim: The ascending genes tended to enrich in HHT-induced downregulated genes (ES<0), while descending genes appeared to be more associated with HHT-induced upregulated genes (ES>0).
source: The results indicated that the ascending genes tended to enrich in HHT-induced downregulated genes (ES<0), while descending genes appeared to be more associated with HHT-induced upregulated genes (ES>0), suggesting that the ability of HHT to reverse the Sigevo was independent of cell type and treatment concentration (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C, Figure 7—source data 1, GSE193897).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The ability of HHT to reverse the Sigevo was independent of cell type and treatment concentration.
source: The results indicated that the ascending genes tended to enrich in HHT-induced downregulated genes (ES<0), while descending genes appeared to be more associated with HHT-induced upregulated genes (ES>0), suggesting that the ability of HHT to reverse the Sigevo was independent of cell type and treatment concentration (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C, Figure 7—source data 1, GSE193897).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the GSEA results presented.

claim: RPL3 had higher expression levels in tumor compared with non-tumor tissues in more than half the clinical cohorts (57.1%).
source: The results showed that RPL3 had higher expression levels in tumor compared with non-tumor tissues in more than half the clinical cohorts (57.1%) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Higher expression of RPL3 indicated worse prognosis.
source: Higher expression of RPL3 also indicated worse prognosis (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: RPL3 was essential for maintaining the survival and growth of all liver cancer cell lines.
source: In addition, leveraging CRISPR-based screening data from Project Achilles (Meyers et al., 2017), we found that RPL3 was essential for maintaining the survival and growth of all liver cancer cell lines (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with a citation to Meyers et al., 2017 and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: HHT had a lower distribution of IC50 values across 482 PRISM cell lines compared with molecular-targeted agents and non-oncology agents.
source: It could be observed that HHT had a lower distribution of IC50 values across 482 PRISM cell lines compared with molecular-targeted agents and non-oncology agents (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In liver cancer cell lines, HHT exhibited a powerful tumor suppressor activity with a median IC50 value of 0.408 μM.
source: Of note, in liver cancer cell lines, HHT exhibited a powerful tumor suppressor activity with a median IC50 value of 0.408 μM, which was numerically lower than that of other three Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved HCC agents (lenvatinib: 0.617 μM; regorafenib: 2.009 μM; sorafenib: 3.348 μM) (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: HHT's median IC50 value was numerically lower than that of lenvatinib (0.617 μM), regorafenib (2.009 μM), and sorafenib (3.348 μM) in liver cancer cell lines.
source: Of note, in liver cancer cell lines, HHT exhibited a powerful tumor suppressor activity with a median IC50 value of 0.408 μM, which was numerically lower than that of other three Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved HCC agents (lenvatinib: 0.617 μM; regorafenib: 2.009 μM; sorafenib: 3.348 μM) (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: HHT could significantly inhibit the growth of xenograft tumors.
source: The result demonstrated that HHT could significantly inhibit the growth of xenograft tumors (Figure 7G and H), with limited drug-related toxicity (Figure 7I).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: HHT treatment showed limited drug-related toxicity in the xenograft model.
source: The result demonstrated that HHT could significantly inhibit the growth of xenograft tumors (Figure 7G and H), with limited drug-related toxicity (Figure 7I).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: HHT could synergize with sorafenib in many conditions, albeit not very remarkable in general.
source: The results suggested that HHT could indeed synergize with sorafenib in many conditions, albeit not very remarkable in general (Figure 7—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: HHT could significantly reduce Ishak scores compared to vehicle controls in the CCL4-induced mouse liver fibrosis model.
source: The results suggested that HHT could significantly reduce Ishak scores and positive area of Sirius Red staining compared to vehicle controls (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: HHT could significantly reduce positive area of Sirius Red staining compared to vehicle controls in the CCL4-induced mouse liver fibrosis model.
source: The results suggested that HHT could significantly reduce Ishak scores and positive area of Sirius Red staining compared to vehicle controls (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: HHT treatment could lead to significant reduction of serum levels of alanine transaminase (ALT) and aspartate transaminase (AST).
source: Besides, HHT treatment could also lead to significant reduction of serum levels of alanine transaminase (ALT) and aspartate transaminase (AST) (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: HHT can impede fibrosis development and partially rescued hepatic function in CCL4-induced mouse model.
source: These observations demonstrated that HHT can impede fibrosis development and partially rescued hepatic function in CCL4-induced mouse model.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented.

claim: After HHT treatments, the expression level of almost all fibrotic genes was downregulated.
source: After HHT treatments, the expression level of almost all fibrotic genes was downregulated (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Figure 8—source data 1, GSE180243).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: HHT could inhibit the protein expression of collagen I and α-SMA.
source: The results showed that HHT could inhibit the protein expression of collagen I and α-SMA as well.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data.

claim: HHT can inhibit the progression of liver fibrosis via suppressing HSC activation.
source: Taken collectively, HHT can inhibit the progression of liver fibrosis via suppressing HSC activation and thus may have certain preventive effects on liver cancer.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented.

claim: HHT may have certain preventive effects on liver cancer.
source: Taken collectively, HHT can inhibit the progression of liver fibrosis via suppressing HSC activation and thus may have certain preventive effects on liver cancer.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing HHT's anti-fibrotic effects.

claim: Inhibition of liver fibrogenesis might prevent the progression of cirrhosis and thereby suppress HCC tumorigenesis.
source: Inhibition of liver fibrogenesis might prevent the progression of cirrhosis and thereby suppress HCC tumorigenesis (Fuchs et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fuchs et al., 2014.

claim: Prevention of HCC development in patients at high risk of primary malignancy rather than treating patients at advanced stages is theoretically the most desirable approach to improve patient prognosis.
source: Notably, in view of the grim prognosis and imperfect treatment modalities of liver cancer, prevention of HCC development in patients at high risk of primary malignancy rather than treating patients at advanced stages is theoretically the most desirable approach to improve patient prognosis (Fujiwara et al., 2018; Nakagawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fujiwara et al., 2018 and Nakagawa et al., 2016.

claim: HHT has been approved by FDA for the treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia.
source: As HHT has been approved by FDA for the treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia, it can be tested directly in clinic without worrying about its safety problem (Kantarjian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kantarjian et al., 2013.

claim: HHT can be tested directly in clinic without worrying about its safety problem.
source: As HHT has been approved by FDA for the treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia, it can be tested directly in clinic without worrying about its safety problem (Kantarjian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on the fact that HHT is already FDA-approved for another indication.
